questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: A range of factors were important to me when choosing my destination. First of all, I was interested in trying to live in a non-European country, as I expected the culture to be different, but I was at the same time determined to attend a well renowned university. I ended up in Seattle as the Northwest Pacific is known to be absolutely beautiful nature wise, but also because I could choose to stay for two quarters, which gave me the opportunity to become familiar with the university, and make lasting friendships. The amazing campus didn't hurt either.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
I had done a lot (a lot..) of emailing beforehand, so I had some good contacts when getting there. The university staff is extremely fast at getting back to you, which is pretty useful as a new student - we're talking the same or next day.

The more difficult part might be figuring out where to look for the information you're in need of. The FIUTS is a nonprofit organization founded on campus which focuses on international relationships, and besides arranging events, they can often point you in the direction needed, whether regarding housing, how to get around, or suggestions on cool hangout spots. If you need information on specific courses, you can email the professor directly.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: As an international student, you'll have to attend an obligatory FIUTS event where you're provided some useful information and welcomed. If you don't need further information during your stay, you can in theory leave it at that. The professors will introduce you to your courses, and most courses will spend a lecture or two on getting you settled with any program you might be required to download.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
There are loads of housing opportunities off campus, your only limitation will be your budget. I found my housing through a friend I made on a hike, who happened to live in a house with a spare room. My friends found housing - if not on campus - through various Facebook groups. If you're currently in search for a place to stay, you might wanna look at:
-	University of Washington (UW) Housing, Subleases, Roommates, Apartments
-	University of Washington (UW) Housing, Sublets & Roommates

I'll recommend living off campus if you're able to, as the prices are much cheaper in an already pretty expensive city. And don't be afraid of asking people you meet! It's a big university, so there'll be a lot of people moving around most year.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's relatively cheaper, but will obviously require some sort of commute. In general, the public transportation is good in Seattle (especially compared to other American cities!), and biking is definitely a possibility too. Most off-campus housing will be offered as a room in a shared house, where you share bathroom and kitchen, but most often have your own room. Many people make a living of renting out houses to students, so you'll probably get a landlord/lady who can be more or less helpful in providing you furniture and overall assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I brought a few personal items to decorate my room such as pictures of friends, which made me more comfortable in my room, as these can be very basic otherwise.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration is easy when you've become familiar with UW's MyPlan page. You'll get a UW netID when accepted at the university, that you need in order to register for courses online. When browsing through courses you can add them to your MyPlan and register from there. It's not the easiest system at first, but when you become a bit acquainted with it, it is actually quite helpful.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Some courses require a system key in order to register, which a professor or the faculty can provide. System keys aren't needed that often though, so most of the time you'll be able to register easily when your registration period begins. If you have any questions regarding the course or if the level is of any concern to you, the professors and TA's are really helpful, and usually get back to you pretty fast.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted, so my main issue was that many courses were scheduled at the same time, requiring me to prioritize. That was honestly a bit annoying, but that way I had an opportunity to sign up for some classes I didn't think of originally.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would recommend spending some time deciding on courses prior to the registration period, as some are filled rather quickly. In my case it wasn't an issue, but depending on your field, it might be to you. UW offers a lot of courses though, so you should be able to get something that interests you, even if your first choice fills up faster than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Please don't worry about the academic level. If you spend as much time on your studies as in Denmark, you'll do absolutely fine, and if you spend less, you'll also get by. As long as you make sure of handing stuff in on time, you won't run into any trouble. I studied at UW as an undergrad student, but ended up taking some master courses, and the level was still suitable. If you do have some concerns though, you can always contact the professor, and they'll be able to guide you.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teacher-student tone is overall as you're used to in Denmark: down to earth, usually first name based, nothing to worry about. Some teachers might prefer being addressed as professor, but they will make that clear early on.

The style of teaching is quite different in a number of ways. For instance, you'll be expected to be doing assignments, exercises, quizzes, and post on discussion boards during the quarters, where the amount obviously differs. It can feel a bit overwhelming at first, so if you, like me, prefer your workload presented in an easy and clear way, I found an Excel sheet containing all my tasks a very useful tool.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
-	Introduction to Geographic Information Systems in Forest Resources
-	Rivers and Beaches
-	Remote Sensing of the Environment

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
questions.answer:
-	Application In Geographic Information Systems For The Earth Sciences
-	Exploring The Atmospheric Sciences
-	The Global Carbon Cycle And Climate
-	Professional Environmental Communication

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you like me haven't had remote sensing, I would recommend ‘Remote Sensing of the Environment'. Monika Moskal is an amazing teacher, and the course provides a broad idea of the applications of remote sensing in earth sciences, including some LiDAR and general classification. I also enjoyed ‘The Global Carbon Cycle And Climate', which introduces Python in an manageable way, if you're new to programming.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Concerts, theatres, and such are pretty similar to Danish prices, but food and bars were definitely more expensive than what I expected. For some reason vegetables especially were expensive, so I had some rather unsatisfying meals once in a while, when feeling a bit cheap.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
I had expected to buy a bicycle to save money on transportation, but you'll automatically get charged for the so-called ‘UPass' which provides you with free public transportation in Seattle. The UPass is a bit expensive ($92 pr quarter), but once paid, it's very convenient to have.

Tipping is always expected and is usually around $15-$20. Taxes are not included in the prices you see in stores or restaurants, and you can always pay with card - cash is rarely necessary unless having to pay for the bus.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Considering Covid was still only wearing off, I thought the different clubs and the IMA (sport building) did a pretty good job of entertaining. The UW offers a broad range of clubs that you should definitely check out.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The organizations FIUTS and Circle, both located at campus, offer international students an array of social, get-to-know-each-other activities which are especially nice to attend in the beginning. The IMA has some fitness classes you can sign up for, and then there are the student led clubs that you can join.
I really joined the Climbing Club which also offers hiking trips. As you need a car to get to the good trails, joining such a club is a must if you have a desire to go hiking. The Lettuce Eating Club is a great concept if you like lettuce, and the Board Game Club is also fun if you're a board game geek. I also joined The Salsa Club, where I met some cool people who I went dancing with in the weekends. You can browse around this link to find a club that suits you:
https://huskylink.washington.edu/
. Some of them have Facebook groups or Discord accounts where they post additional information.
You should also look into what sports are in season (ex.: autumn = American football, spring = baseball) as American universities are really into sports. I went to a few games and had a great time.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: While in Seattle I ended up taking sailing lessons, which I absolutely loved! Seattle has some big lakes, so if you're looking to get into sailing, I would recommend that! At The Little Red Hen they have free linedance every Monday night, and a number of bars have trivia nights which are a lot of fun too! Seattle is also known for its grunge music, so if you enjoy concerts that's a must. If you like cats you could also check out Neko Cat Café. Their Instagram is cute.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: If someone were to visit Seattle, I would recommend some of the parks such as Discovery Park (especially the lighthouse), Golden Gardens (where you if lucky can see sealions), Union Bay Natural Area, and the Arboretum Waterfront Trail. If going out, The Mountaineering Club is a cool rooftop bar with fancy cocktails at the University Avenue which is definitely worth a visit. Seattle also has a number of farmers markets whereof I especially liked the one in Ballard, open Sunday mornings. Another site worth mentioning is the Ballard Locks where you can also see the fish ladders. If you're going in December, you should visit Candy Cane Lane, which is a cute, tiny street in Ravenna decorated with Christmas lights.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Supermarkets are bigger and further apart, the houses are bigger, the measurements are all different to the ones you're used to, and you need a car if leaving the city, but other than that Seattle isn't that odd. The jetlag probably caused the biggest disturbance, but that will wear off quickly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: As an international student, you'll more easily interact with other international students, as they are the ones in search of new friends. The American friends I made were housemates, friends' housemates, FIUTS staff, or people I met rather randomly when going out. If being open and taking initiative, it will happen naturally.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I found it a bit annoying that not having a car would sometimes pose an issue, which is why it's clever to joining a club or rent a car with friends, when going somewhere.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really liked the American openness and being greeted whenever entering a store or paying for something. I find myself in need of a Danish equivalent of “How're you?” now..

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
-	Rain clothes
-	Hiking boots
-	Slippers

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The campus has a lot of great study spaces to discover if you prefer studying at campus. You can even reserve a private study room if in need, but this usually requires you to do so a day or two in advance.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed having an actual campus, as it somehow makes you feel as a part of a large community. Also, I generally just loved getting to know so many amazing and lovely people from all over, as I have developed a better understanding of a lot of countries, as well as now having the option to visit people from here and there.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I had some personal challenges in the very beginning, as my partner and I broke up, making me considering going home for a few weeks - but I'm so glad I didn't! If you come across something similar, let your housemates know so they can look out for you, keep yourself busy with fun stuff, and call your friends and family back home. Don't let it ruin your exchange, because you rock for doing it in the first place!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy! Time passes so quickly and before you know it, you're back home missing all your new friends. Have fun, make friends, and challenge yourself.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
